newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Land hunger seen as danger to HK harbour.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Land hunger seen as danger to HK harbour.

text.p: Relentless land reclamation threatens to turn Hong Kong's famed panoramic harbour into a narrow, useless "river", Green lobbyists are warning the government of China's newest and richest region.
They say demands by land-hungry big business pose a risk to the deep-water Victoria Harbour, one of the world's great free ports, and could destroy an asset that made Hong Kong rich.
Coastal reclamation expanded Hong Kong's territory from the sea by nearly 20 percent in 156 years of British rule and the expansion is set to go on despite the colony's return to China.
Even Britain's historic July 1 handover to Beijing occurred in a Convention Centre built on an off-shore man-made island.
Hong Kong means "Fragrant Harbour" in Chinese but environmentalists say pollution has destroyed any fragrance.
Next to go may be the wide-sweeping harbour, which is the world's busiest container port and a tourist magnet worth billions of dollars.
Around a quarter million ocean-going vessels use the harbour yearly, but developers in the skyscraper-dotted waterfront want to push the land further out towards major shipping lanes.
BUSINESS FUELS HK DRIVE FOR MORE LAND
Business remains the engine driving ultra-capitalist, crowded Hong Kong where land is like gold, making property values among the world's highest.
Ecologists fear this expansion could make a channel of Victoria Harbour, long regarded as the only natural resource in Hong Kong besides the hard-working 6.4 million population.

Despite opposition by some legislators, environmentalists and concerned citizens, government-run reclamation is providing land for a huge new airport, commercial development and housing, as well as a base for the People's Republic of China navy.
The environmental group, Friends of the Earth, fears the impact of reclamation since 1994 when some main projects began.
"From an ecological point of view, the Victoria Harbour is quite a degraded habitat. There's no natural coastal line left anyway. And the water quality is very poor," said spokeswoman Lisa Hopkinson.
Former parliamentarian Christine Loh, a deputy chairman of the Society for Protection of the Harbour, says reclamation will cause permanent damage while making profit for the government.

"The harbour is our common asset. Once it is reclaimed, it will be gone forever. It's difficult to measure our loss in terms of money. But the government can earn a lot from reclamation by selling the reclaimed land," said Loh.
A campaign by the organisation a few months ago collected nearly 150,000 signatures objecting to reclamation.
TYCOONS SEE RECLAMATION AS INEVITABLE
But shipping tycoons like Dr Frank Chao, president of Wah Kwong Shipping Holdings and a council member of the Port Development Board, disagree.
"As a member of the Port Development Board for a long time, I support all these (reclamation) activities.
"And the government has conducted plenty of research to ensure that the problems caused by reclamation will be acceptable before taking any action," said Chao.
He emphasised that for Hong Kong to remain an East Asia commercial and financial hub, reclamation is the only solution to the shortage of usable land.
The Hong Kong Tourist Association, agreeing that projects should consider environmental issues, thinks reclamation plans can benefit tourism by creating new facilities and hotels.
Surprisingly, the cross-harbour passenger ferry service says reclamation would not necessarily affect its business.
"The most important problem related to reclamation is safety. Since the harbour is not as wide as before, the pilots have to be very careful," said Liliane Chen, a ferry executive.
More land, less water -- in a century Hong Kong has clawed back 6,000 hectares (15,000 acres) of land from the sea, according to official figures.
Hong Kong, at the southern tip of China, comprises a chunk of mainland and a cluster of islands whose shape under reclamation keeps changing, requiring new maps to be issued every few years.
